verified_claims_summary: Upshaw et al. (2022) studied 73 college students using a modified Navon letter task with smartphone-notification and control sounds. Participants responded more slowly on notification-sound trials; the behavioral analysis included 69 participants and the ERP analysis included 54. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0277220))

The same study found larger N2-related ERP responses for smartphone-notification sounds and interpreted them as greater recruitment of cognitive-control processes. The article’s statement that participants continued the task without checking a screen is consistent with the experimental procedure. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0277220))

Skowronek, Seifert and Lindberg (2023) reported a final sample of 42 college students. Phones in the smartphone condition were switched off and placed on the desk, while phones in the comparison condition were switched off and placed in another room; participants did not look at or pick up the phones. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36256-4))

The reported differences are accurate: mean attention-performance scores were 99.71 with the phone present versus 108.95 without it, a difference of 9.24 points; mean work-speed scores were 98.48 versus 108.57, a difference of 10.09 points. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36256-4))

The 2018 Pew Research Center figures are accurate: 72% of U.S. teens said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications as soon as they woke up, and 56% associated not having their cellphone with at least one of anxiety, loneliness or being upset. ([pewresearch.org](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2018/08/22/how-teens-and-parents-navigate-screen-time-and-device-distractions/))
sources: Skowronek, Seifert and Lindberg, Scientific Reports (2023): ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36256-4))
result.notes: 記事の中心的な具体的主張は一次論文およびPew Research Centerの公式調査と整合する。なお、Scientific Reports研究は「単に通知をミュートした電話」ではなく、電源を切った電話を用いていたため、「silent phone」という表現には若干の用語上の簡略化がある。ただし記事本文は電源オフであったことと、ミュート自体を解決策として検証していないことを明記しており、重大な誤りとは判断しない。
